## The trap

Every `bin/*.sh` in this repo runs under `set -uo pipefail`. Under `pipefail` this
extremely common idiom is **broken**:

```bash
{ readlink -f "/proc/$pid/cwd"; tr '\0' ' ' <"/proc/$pid/cmdline"; } \
  | grep -qaE "$PATTERN" && owned=1     # ← misfires on a MATCH
```

`grep -q` exits the instant it finds the first matching line and closes its stdin.
The upstream producer (here `tr`, still writing the second line) then takes **SIGPIPE**
and exits non-zero. With `pipefail`, a pipeline's status is the last non-zero command's
status — so the **whole pipeline reports non-zero even though grep matched**. The
trailing `&& owned=1` (or `&& return 0`) therefore **never runs**, and a genuine match is
read as "no match".

Counter-intuitively it only bites on a **match** (the short-circuit path). A non-match
makes grep read the input to EOF, the producer finishes cleanly, the pipeline is
`grep`'s exit `1`, and everything behaves. So the bug is a silent **false-negative** that
passes casual testing (the non-match case works) and only fails the case you care about.

Real incident (EI-14500): the live-federation gate's leaked-sidecar reaper used exactly
this shape in its rig-ownership check. Under the gate's own `pipefail`, every owned orphan
read as "not owned", so `reap_gate_sidecars` `continue`d past all of them and reaped
nothing — the orphan leak the trap was written to close persisted anyway.

## The fix

Capture the producer output into a variable, then grep a **here-string** — no pipeline,
so no SIGPIPE and no `pipefail` interference:

```bash
info="$(readlink -f "/proc/$pid/cwd" 2>/dev/null; tr '\0' ' ' <"/proc/$pid/cmdline" 2>/dev/null)"
grep -qaE "$PATTERN" <<<"$info" && owned=1     # single command → exit is grep's own
```

A single command with input redirection returns grep's exit status directly; `pipefail`
governs pipelines (`|`), not `<<<`.

## Other safe forms

- `grep -qm1` doesn't help — it still short-circuits; the SIGPIPE is on the *producer*.
- If you must keep the pipeline, wrap just that line: `set +o pipefail; … | grep -q …; rc=$?; set -o pipefail`.
- Or put the producer last: `grep -qaE "$PATTERN" <(producer)` (process substitution — grep is the pipeline's only stage).

The capture-then-here-string form is the clearest and is what the codebase now uses.
Watch for this whenever you write `{ … } | grep -q … && …` (or `| grep -q … || …`) in a
`set -o pipefail` script.
